inline.s: He has used the Japanese secret-service organs to train certain personnel in preparation for a counterattack on the mainland; he established a temple of the Primal Vow school in Taiwan, and so the Primal Vow school went to Taiwan and was spread there. Later, when Chiang Kai-shek’s hopes of counterattacking the mainland came to nothing, the Primal Vow school nevertheless gained a certain influence in Taiwan. The Japanese devils’ determination to destroy our China will never cease; their wolfish ambition will never disappear. He therefore transmitted the Primal Vow school through Taiwan to Hong Kong — because directly entering the mainland is impossible; it cannot come straight in — so shifting ground, transmitting it from Hong Kong back to the mainland, slowly spreading it back. First, from the ideological side, washing and brainwashing your mind. Moreover, there is a saying in Japan, reported in many places online: if you but establish on the mainland a temple propagating the Primal Vow school, the Japanese side will contribute ten million yuan. To build your temple, they contribute at least ten million, in covert support. Wherein lies the purpose? To have you build a great temple, expand its influence, occupy the sphere of belief of the common people, and have them accept its ideological indoctrination — this serves that purpose. If a nation loses its own thought and its own culture, that nation is already dead in name but alive in substance. So the Japanese devils, having not won on the battlefield, seek by every means to destroy you — first in religion, in league with the United States. Why cry “freedom of religious belief”? They mean: once I have brought the Primal Vow school in, you cannot touch me. If you touch me, you are obstructing freedom of religious belief. So this is deeply calculated. And it is brandishing the Buddhist
banner

. For Japan’s Shintō (the Way of the Gods) could never be introduced into China. As for his Primal Vow school, the great masters of our mainland have likewise opposed it; he therefore takes a detour through Taiwan and Hong Kong to bring it back in, corrupting you economically, exploiting the current one-sided pursuit of economic development on the part of the Chinese, and cultivating internal contradictions in China in order to disintegrate it. Therein lies his purpose. Slowly, slowly, he comes to control the thinking of our common people.

In Changsha I came into contact with many believers of the Primal Vow school; they recite “Namo Amitabha Buddha,” and whenever they greet anyone it is “Namo Amitabha Buddha.” One of their believers chatted with me. I said “Amitabha Buddha,” and he said “Namo Amitabha Buddha.” When I pronounced “Amitabha Buddha” once, he said, “That won’t do — to recite merely ‘Amitabha Buddha’ is to shed the Buddha’s blood.” He said “Namo Amitabha Buddha” cannot be broken apart; if you leave off the two characters “Namo,” you shed the Buddha’s blood

I said, What is “shedding the Buddha’s blood”? What is the meaning of “Namo”? What is the meaning of “Amitabha Buddha”? He could not answer, because he simply does not understand the meaning of Amitabha Buddha. “Amitabha Buddha” is the complete name of the Buddha’s virtuous qualities; “Namo” means that we take refuge in, revere, and bow to Amitabha Buddha. Therefore when Master Yinguang urged the recitation of the Buddha’s name, it too began with the six characters. Why six characters? Because at that point we had no self-power and lacked self-confidence; so we take refuge in, revere, and bow to Amitabha Buddha, seeking the protective power of his blessing. The purpose lies in this — hence one recites “Namo Amitabha Buddha.” But after one has recited to the end, if faith arises and one still recites “Namo Amitabha Buddha,” then one forever does not believe in oneself, forever believes only in an external Amitabha Buddha, with no Amitabha Buddha within oneself — this is called a heretical path. When we begin to recite, we are ordinary beings weighted by karmic hindrances, so we must rely on Amitabha Buddha — rely on an external Amitabha Buddha — “Namo Amitabha Buddha,” taking refuge in, revering, and bowing to him, so that he blesses us. But once one has recited until the self-Buddha appears, to still recite “Namo” is to forever exclude oneself from Amitabha Buddha, forever incapable of attaining Buddhahood. When you have recited to the end, you no longer need “Namo” — why still take refuge? Because I have already recited the self-Buddha into appearance; I am myself originally Amitabha Buddha. Then one can directly recite the name. So at the beginning, when the power is insufficient, one adds “Namo.” Reciting to the end, if you still must have “Namo,” then you can never enter into the realm of Amitabha Buddha. Every person is Amitabha Buddha — the body of the Dharma-realm, the body of the cosmos, present nowhere and everywhere; we are originally a portion of Amitabha Buddha. Amitabha Buddha is a whole, and we are a portion of the whole. Are we not within Amitabha Buddha? At the beginning, because we cannot recognize ourselves, we add “Namo”; at the end, once we have recognized ourselves, why still seek from without? Amitabha Buddha is right at this present moment. Then the two characters “Namo” can be removed — no longer needed — cutting straight through to the point, directly being Amitabha Buddha. So sometimes I make a joke and say, when you meet a person of that Primal Vow school, one glance tells you he is a heretic. Why? Because when we greet people

it is “Amitabha Buddha.” That means you too are Amitabha Buddha, and I too am Amitabha Buddha. But he, “Namo Amitabha Buddha, Namo Amitabha Buddha,” is always reciting; it means: you are Amitabha Buddha, I must take refuge in, revere, and bow to you — and so he himself is not Amitabha Buddha. He can forever never be the same as Amitabha Buddha — is this not seeking the Dharma outside the mind? If one always recites “Namo Amitabha Buddha,” one forever does not believe that one can attain Buddhahood, forever outside Amitabha Buddha. That is precisely why it is called an external (heretical) path — and so it is a heretical path attached to Buddhism.

The above is an analysis of it in theory. In fact, having been paying attention to it in this period, I deliberately looked at their “Primal Vow Mountain” in Anhui. The books written by the masters on the mountain are riddled with holes in their theory. For example, they dare not acknowledge the successive patriarchs; they only drag out Master Shandao of the Tang dynasty, yet the Primal Vow taught by Master Shandao and their “Primal Vow” are entirely mismatched — they merely borrowed the name of Master Shandao. Then why does it gain so many followers? Because sentient beings are superstitious
unable to tell the true from the false, helpless
What he teaches is a counterfeit Dharma; he brandishes the Buddhist
banner

, dragging out Master Shandao. How many of the ordinary public have ever read Master Shandao’s writings? They have not; you do not know what Master Shandao actually said. So whatever Primal Vow Mountain says is taken as it stands. One only knows that Master Shandao is a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, and that what he said cannot be wrong. The ordinary public all have this mentality; where would they have the ability and the energy to understand the Four-Fascicle Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra that Master Shandao wrote? Not having read it, they say it is so — they say Master Shandao said exactly this — and you think it is right, and they drag you along with them. And there is another point: Anhui Primal Vow Mountain built a very large temple, with local support, because they have money. And where does the money come from — Hong Kong and Taiwan. Is it really Hong Kong and Taiwan? That is why I want to trace out this cause; I want to trace it back to Japan — their money comes from Japan, laundered through Taiwan and Hong Kong. Including the Zizhulin in Gaogiao town, Changsha County, near us — within a few years it flourished enormously and even received commendations from the relevant quarters. Why? Because it has money! Whoever has money has ability. They do not care whether you are orthodox or heretical; they only look at the money. The Purple Bamboo Mountain built up a great size within a few years; where did its funds come from? It says they came over from Taiwan and Hong Kong — “From Japan!” I tell you.

So we, as Chinese people, if we lack even this vigilance, then in the end something will go wrong and we will not know how it happened. Do not believe their devilish talk, I tell you! The Primal Vow school by no means has any genuine good will toward us — that is absolutely impossible, I tell you! Because the general public has not studied it,
Japan’s

culture is itself a wolfish culture bearing the character of aggression; only our Chinese culture is the true culture of harmony. To imagine it will be harmonious with you is impossible. Only when we are stronger than it can we truly achieve harmony — and we will not aggress against others. Moreover, regarding this Master Jingzong himself: he is fundamentally a false monk who, in collusion with the imported Japanese Primal Vow school, was expelled from the gate of Mount Jiuhua by his own teacher, the Great Master Rende — the monk Shi Shengsu

His — that Anhui Hongyuan Temple, deliberately Japanese in style — deceives ignorant believers, propagates wrong views, and has fabricated many groundless, unreliable cases of rebirth. The whole temple has no public account. It is precisely from this point that I investigated him: a temple as large as it is, yet there is no public account — only a personal account of his own, and several bank accounts are all personal. When Shi Jingzong wants others to send money, it goes directly into his personal account. With a temple this large and such great capital flows, how can one open the accounts in a personal name? This is simply not in accord with the Dharma.

With a personal account, you alone can take as you please; there is no one to supervise you. One person is private; three persons make it public. So if you build such a great temple — as a Dharma-propagating place where one preaches the Dharma — do you not know even the basic national financial system? At the very least, a temple as large as the Hongyuan Temple should open an account in the name of the Hongyuan Temple — a public account — so that mutual supervision is exercised; this is the most basic thing. So on this very point as well, he is not in accord with the Dharma.

Not to mention that his funds are Japanese-supported, and that what he propagates is an extreme other-power domination, the thought of the Shintō way of the gods, a typical heretical path attached to Buddhism. On the one hand, they aim to destroy the Buddha-Dharma, abolishing the precepts as teacher; on the other, they prepare ideologically for a future alliance of the United States and Japan to bring down Chinese culture. Therein lies their purpose. Let us never believe that they have any good intent; to understand a bit of Japanese culture is to make it clear: Japanese culture is a kind of transformed, servile culture, and it is deeply inferior! Why is it inferior? Because it has no culture of its own; it was influenced from childhood by our China and cannot shake off China’s shadow. In the Meiji era of modern times, why did it so avidly study the West? It wanted to throw off China. Because the roots of its culture come from China, from our Confucianism and Buddhism — all transmitted over from us. Its nation has a sense of inferiority; the whole Japanese nation has a sense of inferiority. It always wants to emphasize that it is stronger than others. Yet it cannot shake off China’s influence, and so it studies the West — but in its bones the roots still come from China, and learning the West it cannot imitate it aright, and so a distorted mentality arises. Yet it dares not acknowledge it; having erred, it dares not acknowledge it. It aggressed against China, yet to its death it is unwilling to acknowledge it. Of such a country, can you hold good thoughts? Japan holds no good impression in my book. So that Primal Vow school, transmitted by them and heavily tinged with politics, is something that we as Buddhists must resolutely oppose; we must see clearly its essence and not be led by the nose. May it not come to the point of a knife at your neck, and you still die confused and utterly willing. As Buddhists, we must understand this clearly.

In our present society, some people put money above all; they care not what Dharma-gate it is, only about present profit. But ultimately what heretical doctrines corrupt is our Buddhism — they destroy our Buddhism. So in this present situation, when we Buddhists stand up and oppose the Primal Vow school, some may say that is an internal matter of Buddhism — that we Buddhists are internally disharmonious.

This is not a matter of internal disharmony. I earnestly remind everyone: it bears on the question of cultural aggression, on severing the roots of your culture — this is not a small matter. This so-called Japanese Shandao-lineage Primal Vow heretical doctrine, propagated chiefly by the abbot of the Anhui Japanese-based Hongyuan Temple (the monk Shengsu, that is, Master Jingzong, publicly expelled from the Buddhist order by the Great Master Rende, the head abbot of the whole of Mount Jiuhua) and by the Taiwanese Master Huijing, who once studied in Japan, has entered China and is propagandizing on a grand scale, turning Amitabha Buddha into a god, an externalized deity, a God, with the further aim of abolishing the Buddhist precepts and denying and rejecting the three studies of precepts, meditation, and wisdom —
in order to
brandish Buddhism’s
banner —
this harm is very, very great

And our Buddhism itself must also reflect internally: for not having worked to raise its own quality, not preaching the Dharma, not spreading the Way, not carrying out the work of right-faith education in the Dharma, so that heretical doctrines and external paths have seized the gap and taken advantage, causing heresies to flourish
and even causing some of the temples within our Buddhism to degenerate into sites of superstition.
